definition: A distance transform, also known as distance map or distance field, is a derived representation of a digital image.
details: The choice of the term depends on the point of view on the object in question: whether the initial image is transformed into another representation, or it is simply endowed with an additional map or field. Distance fields can also be signed, in the case where it is important to distinguish whether the point is inside or outside of the shape. The map labels each pixel of the image with the distance to the nearest obstacle pixel. A most common type of obstacle pixel is a boundary pixel in a binary image. See the image for an example of a Chebyshev distance transform on a binary image. Usually the transform/map is qualified with the chosen metric. For example, one may speak of Manhattan distance transform, if the underlying metric is Manhattan distance. Common metrics are: Euclidean distance Taxicab geometry, also known as City block distance or Manhattan distance. Chebyshev distance There are several algorithms to compute the distance transform for these different distance metrics, however the computation of the exact Euclidean distance transform (EEDT) needs special treatment if it is computed on the image grid. Applications are digital image processing (e.g., blurring effects, skel

explainer.lead: A distance transform turns an image into a map of distances, giving every pixel a value for how far it is from the nearest obstacle. This makes spatial relationships inside an image explicit and supports image-processing effects such as blurring.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a grid of squares with a few squares marked as fences. Every other square gets a number saying how far away the nearest fence is. You can count distances in different ways, just as you can walk along city streets or measure straight across the grid.
tiers.practitioner: Choose the obstacle set, commonly boundary pixels in a binary image, and qualify the result by the metric used, such as Manhattan, Chebyshev, or Euclidean distance. Use a signed field when inside and outside must be distinguished. Exact Euclidean distance transforms on an image grid need special treatment rather than being handled as an interchangeable grid calculation.
tiers.paperLevel: For an image domain Ω and obstacle set O, the transform assigns D(x) = min_{o ∈ O} d(x, o) to each pixel x ∈ Ω; O commonly consists of boundary pixels in a binary image. A signed variant additionally distinguishes whether a point lies inside or outside the shape. Manhattan, Chebyshev, and Euclidean metrics produce different maps, and exact Euclidean computation on an image grid needs special treatment.

explainer.example: In a 5×5 binary image where only the centre pixel is an obstacle, a Chebyshev distance transform labels its eight immediate neighbours 1. Every pixel on the outer border receives the label 2.

usedIn.name: Digital image processing
usedIn.detail: Provides a derived distance representation that image-processing operations can use.

usedIn.name: Blurring effects
usedIn.detail: Uses per-pixel distances to obstacles as spatial information for image-processing blur effects.

explainer.intuition: Instead of recording only which pixels belong to an object or obstacle, a distance transform records how close every pixel is to one. The resulting map makes nearness and remoteness directly readable as numbers.
howItWorks: Start with a digital image and identify its obstacle pixels.
Commonly use boundary pixels of a binary image as those obstacles.
Choose a metric such as Manhattan, Chebyshev, or Euclidean distance.
Label each pixel with its distance to the nearest obstacle pixel.
Optionally add a sign to distinguish points inside and outside the shape.
explainer.whyItMatters: It converts shape and obstacle locations into an explicit spatial measurement at every pixel. That representation is useful in digital image processing, including blurring effects, while signed fields also retain the inside-versus-outside distinction.
misconceptions: It is not a single metric: Manhattan, Chebyshev, and Euclidean distance transforms produce different values.
It is not necessarily signed: signs are added only when inside and outside must be distinguished.
Exact Euclidean distance on an image grid is not automatically handled by the same straightforward computation as other metrics.
